fields.title: Leviticus
fields.subtitle: Vayikra, “And he called”
fields.description: The third book of the Bible, called in Hebrew Vayikra from its first word, “And he called”: the LORD calling to Moses from the tent where his glory has just come to dwell. It teaches a rescued people how to come near to a holy God and live. Burnt offerings and peace offerings, the hand laid on the animal’s head, priests ordained in fire and glory, and the strange fire of Nadab and Abihu; clean and unclean; the Day of Atonement, with one goat for the LORD and one sent away into the wilderness carrying the people’s sins; “The life of every creature is in its blood”; and then holiness carried into fields, markets and courts, the command to love your neighbour as yourself, the festivals of Israel’s year, and the Jubilee that announces freedom in the land. In the Open Word Bible, a new translation from the Hebrew given freely to the public domain, with an introduction to the book’s shape and meaning and a conclusion on where to read next.

qa.question: What is the book of Leviticus?
qa.answer: The third book of the Bible and of the five books of Moses. Its Hebrew name, Vayikra, “And he called”, is its first word; the name Leviticus comes, through Latin, from the Greek translation and refers to the tribe of Levi, from which the priests came. Set entirely at Mount Sinai, its twenty-seven chapters teach Israel how to live with the holy God who has come to dwell among them: offerings (1–7), the priests (8–10), clean and unclean (11–15), the Day of Atonement (16), and a holy life, holy times and the land (17–27).

qa.question: Who wrote the book of Leviticus?
qa.answer: The book presents its laws as given by the LORD to Moses at Sinai (27:34), and Jewish and Christian tradition has received it as one of the five books of Moses. Many scholars think it was shaped by Israel’s priests over a long period and took its final form after the exile; others argue that much of its content is very old. Christians hold a range of views on how it came together, while receiving it as Scripture and reading it, with the letter to the Hebrews, as a witness to Christ.

qa.question: What are the offerings in Leviticus?
qa.answer: Chapters 1–7 describe five: the burnt offering, given wholly to God on the altar; the grain offering of flour, oil and salt; the peace offering, a meal shared by God, the priests and the worshiper; the sin offering, for sins done unintentionally and for impurity; and the guilt offering, for wrongs that could be repaid, with a fifth added. The worshiper laid a hand on the animal’s head, so that it would “make atonement for them” (1:4), and the poor could bring birds or flour instead of a lamb. Leviticus says that God himself gave the blood for atonement (17:11), and requires confession of sin (5:5).

qa.question: What is the Day of Atonement, and what is the scapegoat?
qa.answer: The most solemn day of Israel’s year, on the tenth day of the seventh month (Leviticus 16; 23:26–32), still kept by Jews as Yom Kippur. Only then could the high priest enter the Most Holy Place, with blood, to cleanse the sanctuary and make atonement for the people. Two goats were chosen by lot, one “for the LORD”, offered as a sin offering, and one “for Azazel”, over whose head the high priest confessed all the people’s sins before it was sent into the wilderness. Older English Bibles called it the scapegoat. Azazel’s meaning is uncertain. The letter to the Hebrews reads the day as a picture of Christ entering heaven itself with his own blood (Hebrews 9).

qa.question: Do Christians have to keep the laws of Leviticus?
qa.answer: Christians generally agree that the sacrifices and priesthood of Leviticus are fulfilled in Christ, the high priest who offered himself once for all (Hebrews 7–10), and that its food laws no longer divide Jew from Gentile (Mark 7:19; Acts 10). Many have also distinguished moral laws, which still bind, from ceremonial and civil laws given for Israel; others prefer to say that the whole law is fulfilled in Christ and read through him. Either way, the New Testament keeps Leviticus’s call to holiness (1 Peter 1:16) and its command to love your neighbour as yourself (19:18), which Jesus called the second great commandment.

fields.title: Introduction
fields.body_html:
You must be holy to me, because I, the LORD, am holy. I have set you apart from the other peoples so that you will belong to me.

— Leviticus 20:26

Many plans to read the whole Bible come to grief in Leviticus. After the drama of Exodus, the reader meets chapter after chapter of sacrifices, priests, skin diseases and food laws, and wonders what any of it has to do with them. Yet an old Jewish custom had children begin their study of Scripture here, and the letter to the Hebrews cannot explain what Jesus has done without it. Leviticus is the book that teaches what it means for a holy God to live among his people. Once you see that, it becomes one of the most searching books in the Bible.

In Hebrew it is called Vayikra, “And he called”, from its first word. The name we use comes, through Latin, from the ancient Greek translation, and means “the Levitical book”, after the tribe of Levi, from which the priests came. Both names point to the same scene. Exodus ended with the glory of the LORD filling the tabernacle, so that even Moses could not go in. Leviticus begins with God calling to Moses from inside it: “From the tent of meeting the LORD called to Moses and spoke to him.” And the first thing he speaks of is how an Israelite may bring “an animal to the LORD as an offering”.

Notice that word “offering”. In Hebrew it comes from the verb “to bring near”. The God who has come to live among his people now tells them how they may come near to him. Everything in the book, the altar, the priests, the washings, the festivals, serves that one purpose.

The shape of the book

Leviticus has almost no story. The whole book is set at Mount Sinai, in the month after the tabernacle was finished, and it is nearly all speech: “The LORD spoke to Moses” is its constant refrain. But it is carefully built, and its plan is worth knowing before you begin:

  • offerings and sacrifices (chapters 1–7)
  • the priests ordained, and the first day of worship (8–10)
  • clean and unclean (11–15)
  • the Day of Atonement (16)
  • a holy people: life, worship and the land (17–27)

The Day of Atonement stands at the centre, and the book turns on it. Before it, the focus is on the sanctuary: how God’s house can be kept and cleansed. After it, the focus widens to the whole of life: how God’s people can be holy in their homes, their fields, their markets and their courts. Scholars often call chapters 17–26 the Holiness Code, from its great repeated command, “You must be holy, because I, the LORD your God, am holy.”

Offerings: coming near

The first seven chapters describe five kinds of offering. The burnt offering is given wholly to God, turned into smoke on the altar, “a soothing aroma to the LORD.” The grain offering is a gift of flour and oil, always with salt, “the salt of your God’s covenant”. The peace offering is a shared meal, in which part goes to God, part to the priests, and the rest is eaten by the worshiper and his household. The sin offering deals with sins done unintentionally, and with impurity. The guilt offering deals with wrongs that can be repaid, and requires that the worshiper pay back what was taken, “with a fifth of its value added”.

Again and again, the worshiper does something with his own hands:

The worshiper is to lay their hand on the head of the burnt offering, which will then be accepted for them and make atonement for them.

— Leviticus 1:4

The animal stands in for the person. Its life is given, and the one who brings it is accepted. Readers have long noticed, too, how carefully the law makes room for the poor: whoever cannot afford a lamb may bring two birds, and whoever cannot afford birds may bring flour. When Mary came to the temple after Jesus was born, Luke says, she brought “a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons”, the offering of a poor family.

Two things are easy to miss. First, sacrifice in Leviticus is not a way of buying God off. He is the one who gives it: “I have given the blood to you to make atonement on the altar for your lives.” Second, the sacrifices cover sins of weakness and ignorance, and wrongs that can be confessed and repaid, but not defiant, high-handed sin. They require confession: “Whoever is guilty in any of these ways must confess the sin they have committed.” The book never imagines that ritual can stand in for a changed heart.

Priests, fire and glory

In chapters 8–9 Moses ordains Aaron and his sons as priests, washing them, clothing them, anointing them and marking them with blood. On the eighth day Aaron offers sacrifices for the first time, and blesses the people, and God answers:

Fire went out from before the LORD and devoured the burnt offering and the fat portions lying on the altar. When all the people saw it, they cried out with joy and bowed down with their faces to the ground.

— Leviticus 9:24

And then, on that very day, disaster. Two of Aaron’s sons, Nadab and Abihu, offer “an improper fire, one he had not commanded them to bring.” The same fire comes out from the LORD and devours them. The text does not say exactly what their sin was, and readers have guessed at it ever since. What it does say is what Moses says to his grieving brother: “Through those who come near me I will show that I am holy.” And it adds four of the saddest words in the book: “And Aaron said nothing.”

The story is placed here to teach the reader the stakes. The nearness of God is the greatest gift Israel has, and the most dangerous. That is why the priests are given a task that frames the next chapters: to “tell apart what is holy and what is common, what is unclean and what is clean.”

Clean and unclean

Chapters 11–15 deal with what makes a person unclean, and how they can be made clean again: animals that may and may not be eaten, childbirth, skin disease and mold, and the flows of the body. These chapters are the strangest in the book to modern readers, and it helps to know three things.

First, being unclean is not the same as sinning. A mother who has just given birth is unclean; so is anyone who has touched the dead. Uncleanness was part of ordinary life, and the law gave ways to deal with it. What mattered was that it should not be brought into God’s presence: “so that it does not bring death on them when they defile my tabernacle, which is among them.”

Second, many of the causes of uncleanness have to do with death: a corpse, the loss of blood, a disease that eats away the skin. The God of Israel is the living God, and the laws keep teaching that life and death cannot share the same space. Hardest of all was the life of someone with a serious skin disease, who had to live “outside the camp” and call out, “Unclean, unclean!” It is worth remembering that sentence when you read in the Gospels how Jesus stretched out his hand and touched such a man, and he was made clean.

Third, the food laws marked Israel off from the nations. Chapter 20 ties the two together: Israel must distinguish clean animals from unclean, because God has set Israel apart from the other peoples. Christians have generally read these laws as fulfilled in Christ, who, in Mark’s words, “made all foods clean”, and whose church brings the nations in.

The Day of Atonement

Chapter 16 opens by recalling the death of Aaron’s sons, and then tells Aaron how he may come into the Most Holy Place, where God appears above the mercy seat. Not “at any time he pleases”, but once a year, on the tenth day of the seventh month, after washing and dressing in plain linen, and only with blood.

Two goats are chosen by lot, one “for the LORD” and one “for Azazel”. The first is killed as a sin offering for the people, and its blood is sprinkled on the mercy seat, to cleanse the sanctuary from the impurities of Israel. Then comes the scene that has given the English language the word “scapegoat”:

Aaron is to lay both his hands on the live goat’s head and confess over it all the wrongdoing of the Israelites, all their rebellious acts, all their sins. So he is to place them on the goat’s head, and send it off into the wilderness with a man kept ready for that purpose. The goat will carry all their wrongdoing on itself into a barren land, and the man is to set the goat free in the wilderness.

— Leviticus 16:21–22

No one knows for certain what Azazel means; the word occurs only in this chapter. It may be the name of a wilderness power, or a word for the remote place where the goat is sent. Either way, the picture is clear. Sin is not only covered over. It is carried away, as far as possible from the camp and from God. And the chapter ends with a promise for the whole people:

For on this day atonement will be made for you to cleanse you, so that before the LORD you are clean of all your sins.

— Leviticus 16:30

The letter to the Hebrews reads this day as a picture of Christ, who “entered the sanctuary once for all” with his own blood, not into a copy made by hands but “into heaven itself”.

The life is in the blood

Chapter 17 explains why blood matters so much in Leviticus, and why Israel must never eat it:

The life of every creature is in its blood. I have given the blood to you to make atonement on the altar for your lives, because the blood makes atonement by means of the life that is in it.

— Leviticus 17:11

Blood stands for life, and life belongs to God. Atonement is made by a life given up. That is the thought behind the New Testament’s many sayings about the blood of Christ, and behind Hebrews’ summary of the whole law: “where no blood is shed there is no forgiveness.”

“You must be holy”

From chapter 18 onward, holiness moves out of the sanctuary into everyday life. Israel is not to copy “what is done in the land of Egypt, where you once lived, or what is done in the land of Canaan, where I am bringing you.” Chapter 19 shows what the alternative looks like, and it is one of the richest chapters in the Old Testament. It mixes laws about worship with laws about farming, business and the courts, as though they were all one thing, because in God’s eyes they are:

When you gather in your land’s harvest, do not cut the grain right up to the edges of your field, and do not collect what is left lying after the reapers. Do not go back through your vineyard to take every last cluster, or collect the grapes that drop to the ground. Leave them for the poor and for the outsider. I am the LORD your God.

— Leviticus 19:9–10

Pay workers the same day; do not curse the deaf or trip the blind; do not favour the poor or the powerful in court; keep honest scales. And then, in the middle of it all:

Do not pay back any of your own people with revenge, and do not keep holding a grudge against them. Instead, love your neighbor as yourself. I am the LORD.

— Leviticus 19:18

Jesus called this the second great commandment, Paul says that the whole law comes to its fullness in it, and James calls it “the royal law”. Sixteen verses later Leviticus applies the same words to the foreigner: “You are to love them as yourself, since you yourselves were outsiders in the land of Egypt.” Notice the refrain that closes so many of these laws: “I am the LORD.” Holiness here is not a mood or a feeling. It is a way of treating people, grounded in who God is.

Holy times: festivals, Sabbath and Jubilee

Chapter 23 sets out Israel’s year: the weekly Sabbath, Passover and Unleavened Bread in spring, the offering of the first sheaf, the Festival of Weeks fifty days later, and in the autumn a day of trumpet blasts, the Day of Atonement and the Festival of Booths, when the people live in shelters to remember the wilderness. Christians will recognise Passover, and the fiftieth day, which came to be known by its Greek name, Pentecost.

Chapter 25 widens the Sabbath to the land itself. Every seventh year the fields are to rest. And every fiftieth year is a Jubilee:

Set the fiftieth year apart as holy, and announce freedom in the land for everyone who lives in it. This will be your Jubilee, when each of you goes home to your own property and to your own clan.

— Leviticus 25:10

Debt, poverty and the loss of family land were not allowed to become permanent, because “the land belongs to me. You are only outsiders and residents living with me.” Whether Israel ever kept the Jubilee fully is not known, but its hope runs through the prophets. When Jesus began his ministry in Nazareth, he read from Isaiah of a messenger sent “to announce freedom to the captives” and “to announce the year when the Lord shows favor.”

Blessing, warning and hope

Chapter 26 sets before Israel the blessings of faithfulness and the consequences of rebellion, ending in exile. The blessings reach their height in a promise of presence:

I will set my dwelling place in your midst, and I will not turn from you in loathing. I will go about among you. I will be God to you, and you will be my people.

— Leviticus 26:11–12

Paul quotes these words to the Corinthians: “We, after all, are the temple of the living God.” And even the warnings do not end in despair. If the scattered people confess their sin, God will remember his covenant with Jacob, Isaac and Abraham: “I will not cast them off.”

How to read Leviticus

Read it with Exodus behind you and Hebrews beside you; chapters 9 and 10 of Hebrews draw again and again on Leviticus 16. Do not try to master every detail of every sacrifice on a first reading. Ask instead, in each chapter, what it shows about God: that he is holy, that he wants to be near, that sin and death are serious, and that he provides the way back.

Listen, too, for the refrains. “I am the LORD” closes law after law, as a signature. “Make atonement” and “they will be forgiven” return again and again in the opening chapters, like a promise repeated until it is believed. And notice how often the poor, the outsider, the deaf and the blind appear in a book that seems at first to be only about ritual. Leviticus never separates the worship of God from the care of the neighbour.

Christians have long debated how these laws apply to them. Many have distinguished moral laws, which still bind, from ceremonial laws, fulfilled in Christ, and civil laws, given for Israel as a nation; others prefer to say that the whole law is fulfilled in Christ and read through him. Either way, the New Testament treats Leviticus not as something to be thrown away but as a shadow of the good things to come.

The book itself says that its commands were given by the LORD to Moses at Sinai (27:34), and Jewish and Christian tradition has received it as one of the five books of Moses. Many scholars think it was shaped by Israel’s priests over a long period and reached its final form after the exile; others argue that much of it is very old. Christians hold a range of views on how it came together, while receiving it as Scripture.

About this translation

The text in this edition is the Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Hebrew and given freely to the public domain. It is printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. A few of its choices in Leviticus are worth knowing before you begin.

“The LORD.” Where the Hebrew uses God’s personal name, the four letters often written Yahweh, this translation follows long Jewish and Christian custom and writes “the LORD”.

Offerings and atonement. The five offerings are called the burnt offering, the grain offering, the peace offering, the sin offering and the guilt offering. The priest’s work for the worshiper is “make atonement”, kept in the same words throughout the book, so the reader can follow it.

“Serious skin disease.” The word older Bibles render “leprosy” covers a range of skin conditions, and the same word is used of marks on cloth, leather and walls. The translation calls the first “serious skin disease” and the second “mold”.

Azazel. The goat of chapter 16 is sent “to Azazel”, keeping the Hebrew word, whose meaning is uncertain, rather than the older “scapegoat”.

“The outsider.” The foreigner who lives among Israel, protected by the law, is usually “the outsider living among you”.

For the reasoning behind every sentence of the translation, with the Hebrew beside it, see the Open Word Bible itself at openwordbible.org.

fields.title: Leviticus 1
fields.body_html:
The burnt offering

From the tent of meeting the LORD called to Moses and spoke to him. He said, “Speak to the Israelites and tell them: ‘If one of you brings an animal to the LORD as an offering, it is to come from the herd or from the flock. A burnt offering from the herd must be a male without defect. It is to be brought to the entrance of the tent of meeting, so that the LORD will accept the one who offers it. The worshiper is to lay their hand on the head of the burnt offering, which will then be accepted for them and make atonement for them. The one who brought the young bull is to slaughter it there before the LORD. Aaron’s sons, the priests, are then to present the blood and splash it on every side of the altar that stands at the entrance of the tent of meeting. The worshiper is then to skin the burnt offering and cut it up into its parts. The sons of Aaron the priest are to put fire on the altar and lay wood in order on the fire. Aaron’s sons, the priests, are to set out the pieces on the burning wood of the altar, along with the head and the suet. The internal organs and the legs are to be washed with water, and the priest is to turn the whole animal into smoke on the altar. It is a burnt offering, a food offering, a soothing aroma to the LORD.

If the animal for the burnt offering comes from the flock, from the sheep or the goats, it must be a male without defect. It is to be slaughtered before the LORD on the north side of the altar, and Aaron’s sons, the priests, are to splash its blood on every side of the altar. It is to be cut into its pieces, and the priest is to set them out, with the head and the suet, on the burning wood of the altar. The internal organs and the legs are to be washed with water. The priest is to present all of it and turn it into smoke on the altar. It is a burnt offering, a food offering, a soothing aroma to the LORD.

If someone’s burnt offering to the LORD is a bird, they are to bring a turtledove or a young pigeon. The priest is to take it to the altar. He is to nip off its head and turn the head into smoke on the altar, and the bird’s blood is to be squeezed out against the altar’s side. He is to take out its crop along with its feathers and throw it down on the east side of the altar, at the place for the ashes. Taking it by the wings, he is to tear it open but not split it in two. Then the priest is to turn it into smoke on the altar, on the burning wood. It is a burnt offering, a food offering, a soothing aroma to the LORD.

fields.title: Leviticus 2
fields.body_html:
The grain offering

If anyone brings a grain offering to the LORD as their offering, it must be fine flour. Oil is to be poured over the flour and frankincense placed on it. They are to bring it to Aaron’s sons, the priests. A priest is to scoop out a full handful of the flour and oil, along with all of the frankincense, and turn this memorial portion into smoke on the altar. It is a food offering, a soothing aroma to the LORD. Whatever remains of the grain offering goes to Aaron and his sons, a share that is most holy, taken from the food offerings of the LORD.

When your grain offering is something baked in an oven, it must be of fine flour: cakes made without yeast and mixed with oil, or wafers made without yeast and spread with oil.

If you offer a grain offering cooked on a flat griddle, the fine flour must be mixed with oil and made without yeast. Break it up into crumbs, then pour oil over it. This is a grain offering.

A grain offering that you cook in a deep pan must be made of fine flour and oil. Whichever of these ways your grain offering is made, you are to bring it to the LORD. Once it is handed to the priest, he is to carry it to the altar. From the grain offering the priest is to lift out its memorial portion and turn it into smoke on the altar. It is a food offering, a soothing aroma to the LORD. Whatever remains of the grain offering goes to Aaron and his sons, a share that is most holy, taken from the food offerings of the LORD. No yeast may go into any grain offering you bring to the LORD. Neither yeast nor honey is ever to be turned into smoke as a food offering to the LORD. As an offering of firstfruits you may bring such things to the LORD, but they must not go up on the altar as a soothing aroma. Every grain offering you present must be salted. Never let your grain offering lack the salt of your God’s covenant. Salt is to go with every offering you bring.

Grain offerings of firstfruits

When you present a grain offering of firstfruits to the LORD, it is to be the new grain of the season, freshly ripe ears roasted over the fire and crushed. That is how you present the grain offering of your firstfruits. Add oil to it and place frankincense on top. This is a grain offering. The priest is to take some of the crushed grain and some of the oil, along with all of the frankincense, and turn this memorial portion into smoke as a food offering to the LORD.

fields.title: Leviticus 3
fields.body_html:
The peace offering

If someone’s offering is a peace offering and they present an animal from the herd, it may be male or female, but it must be without defect when they present it before the LORD. The worshiper is to lay their hand on the animal’s head and slaughter it at the entrance of the tent of meeting. Then Aaron’s sons, the priests, are to splash the blood on every side of the altar. From the peace offering the worshiper is to present a food offering to the LORD: the fat that covers the internal organs and all the fat on them, the two kidneys with the fat on them by the lower back, and the long lobe of the liver, which is to be taken out together with the kidneys. Aaron’s sons are to turn these parts into smoke on the altar, laying them over the burnt offering on the wood of the fire. It is a food offering, a soothing aroma to the LORD.

If the peace offering to the LORD comes from the flock, the animal presented may be male or female, but it must be without defect. If the offering is a lamb, the worshiper is to present it before the LORD. The worshiper is to lay their hand on its head and slaughter it in front of the tent of meeting, and Aaron’s sons are to splash its blood on every side of the altar. From the peace offering the worshiper is to present a food offering to the LORD: its fat, that is, the whole fat tail, taken off right at the backbone, the fat that covers the internal organs and all the fat on them, the two kidneys with the fat on them by the lower back, and the long lobe of the liver, which is to be taken out together with the kidneys. The priest is to turn it all into smoke on the altar as food, a food offering to the LORD.

If the offering is a goat, the worshiper is to present it before the LORD. The worshiper is to lay their hand on its head and slaughter it in front of the tent of meeting, and Aaron’s sons are to splash its blood on every side of the altar. From it the worshiper is to present their offering, a food offering to the LORD: the fat that covers the internal organs and all the fat on them, the two kidneys with the fat on them by the lower back, and the long lobe of the liver, which is to be taken out together with the kidneys. The priest is to turn them into smoke on the altar as food, a food offering and a soothing aroma. All the fat belongs to the LORD. Do not eat any fat or any blood. This is a permanent rule for all your generations, wherever you live.’”

fields.title: Leviticus 4
fields.body_html:
The sin offering

The LORD spoke to Moses. He said, “Speak to the Israelites and tell them: ‘Suppose someone sins unintentionally by doing one of the things that the LORD’s commandments say must not be done. If the anointed priest is the one who sins, his sin makes the people guilty as well. For the sin he has committed he is to present to the LORD a young bull without defect, as a sin offering. The bull is to be brought before the LORD at the entrance of the tent of meeting. The priest is to lay his hand on the bull’s head and slaughter it in the LORD’s presence. The anointed priest is to collect some of the bull’s blood and take it inside the tent of meeting. With his finger dipped in the blood, the priest is to sprinkle some of it before the LORD seven times, facing the curtain of the sanctuary. Next the priest is to apply some of the blood to the horns of the altar of fragrant incense, which stands before the LORD inside the tent of meeting. Whatever is left of the bull’s blood he is to pour out at the base of the altar of burnt offering, which stands at the entrance of the tent of meeting. From the bull of the sin offering he is to take off all its fat: the fat that covers the internal organs, all the fat attached to them, the two kidneys with the fat on them by the loins, and the long lobe of the liver, which he is to remove together with the kidneys, just as these are taken off the ox of a peace offering. Then the priest is to turn them into smoke on the altar of burnt offering. As for the rest of the bull, its hide and all its meat, its head and its legs, its internal organs and its dung, the whole bull, he is to carry out of the camp to a ceremonially clean place, where the ashes are poured out. There he is to burn it in a fire of wood. It must be burned where the ashes are poured out.

When the whole congregation sins

If the whole congregation of Israel goes astray without the assembly being aware of it, and they do something that one of the LORD’s commandments says must not be done, they become guilty. Once the sin they committed comes to light, the assembly is to offer a young bull for a sin offering. They are to bring it to the front of the tent of meeting. Before the LORD the elders of the congregation are to lay their hands on the head of the bull, and then the bull is to be slaughtered in the LORD’s presence. The anointed priest is to carry some of the bull’s blood inside the tent of meeting. Dipping his finger in the blood, the priest is to sprinkle it seven times before the LORD, facing the curtain. Some of the blood he is to apply to the horns of the altar inside the tent of meeting, the one that stands before the LORD. All that remains he is to pour out at the base of the altar of burnt offering, which stands at the entrance of the tent of meeting. He is to remove all its fat and turn it into smoke on the altar. He is to deal with this bull exactly as with the first bull for the sin offering. The priest is to make atonement for them in this way, and they will be forgiven. He is then to carry the bull out of the camp and burn it there, the same way the first bull was burned. It is the sin offering for the assembly.

When a leader sins

When a leader sins, doing unintentionally what one of the commandments of the LORD his God says must not be done, he becomes guilty. Or if he is made aware of the sin he committed, he is to bring a male goat without defect as his offering. Laying his hand on the goat’s head, he is to slaughter it before the LORD at the spot where the burnt offering is killed. It is a sin offering. With his finger the priest is to apply some of the sin offering’s blood to the horns of the altar of burnt offering. The rest of the blood he is to pour out at the base of the same altar. He is to turn all its fat into smoke on the altar, as is done with the fat of a peace offering. Through this the priest is to make atonement for him concerning his sin, and he will be forgiven.

When one of the ordinary people sins

If anyone among the ordinary people sins unintentionally by doing something that one of the LORD’s commandments says must not be done, they become guilty. Or if they are made aware of the sin they committed, they are to bring as their offering a female goat without defect, for the sin they have done. The worshiper is to lay a hand on the sin offering’s head and then slaughter the animal where the burnt offerings are killed. The priest is to take some of its blood on his finger and dab it on the horns of the altar of burnt offering. The remainder of its blood he is to pour out at the altar’s base. All its fat is to be removed in the same way as the fat of a peace offering, and the priest is to turn it into smoke on the altar, a soothing aroma to the LORD. When the priest has made atonement for the worshiper in this way, they will be forgiven.

If the sin offering they bring is a lamb, it must be a female without defect. Laying a hand on the head of the sin offering, the worshiper is to slaughter it as a sin offering at the spot where burnt offerings are killed. The priest is to put some of the sin offering’s blood on his finger and apply it to the horns of the altar of burnt offering. All the rest of its blood he is to pour out at the base of the altar. All its fat is to be removed, just as the fat of a lamb is removed for a peace offering. The priest is then to turn the fat into smoke on the altar, on top of the LORD’s food offerings. So the priest is to make atonement for the sin that person has committed, and they will be forgiven.

fields.title: Leviticus 5
fields.body_html:
Sins that call for a sin offering

If someone hears a public call for witnesses made under a curse, and they saw what happened or know about it but do not speak up, they have sinned and will carry their guilt. Or someone may touch anything unclean, such as the dead body of an unclean wild animal, unclean livestock or an unclean creature that swarms, without realizing it. They have become unclean and are guilty. Or someone may come into contact with human uncleanness of any kind that makes a person unclean, and not notice it. Once they learn of it, they are guilty. Or someone may swear without thinking that they will do something, harmful or good, the kind of oath people make in haste, and then forget it. When they realize it, they are guilty in any of these cases. Whoever is guilty in any of these ways must confess the sin they have committed and bring to the LORD what is owed for the sin: a female animal from the flock, a lamb or a goat, as a sin offering. The priest will make atonement for them for their sin. If a lamb is more than they can afford, they may bring the LORD two turtledoves or two young pigeons to pay for their sin. One of them is for a sin offering, and the other for a burnt offering. The priest receives them and first presents the bird for the sin offering. He breaks its neck at the front but does not pull the head off. Some of its blood he is to sprinkle on the side of the altar, and what is left is to be pressed out at the base of the altar. It is a sin offering. He is to offer the second bird as a burnt offering in the prescribed way. Through this the priest makes atonement for them for their sin, and they will be forgiven.

An offering for those who are poor

If even two turtledoves or two young pigeons are beyond their means, the one who sinned is to bring about 2 quarts of fine flour as a sin offering. No oil or frankincense is to be put on it, since it is a sin offering. The flour is brought to the priest. He takes a full handful from it as its memorial portion and turns it into smoke on the altar, with the food offerings to the LORD. It is a sin offering. The priest is to make atonement for them for the sin they committed in any one of these cases; then they will be forgiven. The rest of the flour belongs to the priest, as with the grain offering.’”

The guilt offering

The LORD spoke to Moses. He said, “If anyone sins without intending to and wrongs the LORD in the matter of his holy things, they must bring a ram from the flock with no defect to the LORD as their guilt offering. Its value is set in shekels of silver by the sanctuary shekel. It is a guilt offering. They must also pay back in full what they wrongly kept from the holy things, with a fifth of its value added, and give it to the priest. With the ram of the guilt offering the priest will make atonement for them, and they will be forgiven.

Suppose someone sins by breaking one of the commands of the LORD, doing what must not be done, and is unaware of it. They are guilty all the same and will carry their guilt, and must bring a ram without defect from the flock, of the set value, to the priest as a guilt offering. So the priest will make atonement for them for the error they did not know they had made, and they will be forgiven. It is a guilt offering. They have certainly become guilty before the LORD.”

fields.title: Leviticus 6
fields.body_html:
Paying back what was wrongly taken

The LORD spoke to Moses. He said, “Suppose someone sins and betrays the LORD by deceiving a neighbor: denying that they hold goods the neighbor gave them to keep or as security, or taking the neighbor’s goods by robbery, or extorting from them, or keeping lost property they found and denying it, or taking a false oath about any of the wrongs people commit, then, being guilty of such a sin, they must hand back the goods they seized by robbery or extortion, the deposit placed with them, or the lost item they found, or anything at all that was the subject of their false oath. They must pay it back in full and a fifth more besides, and the owner is to receive it on the day of their guilt offering. They must bring to the priest their guilt offering for the LORD: a ram without defect from the flock, of the set value.

Instructions for the burnt and grain offerings

Before the LORD the priest will make atonement for them, and they will be forgiven for any one of the wrongs that brought them guilt.”

The LORD spoke to Moses. He said, “Give Aaron and his sons this command: ‘These are the instructions for the burnt offering. The burnt offering is to stay on the hearth of the altar all night, until morning, and the altar fire must be kept burning on it. The priest is to put on his linen robe, with linen undergarments next to his body. Then he is to take up the ashes left when the fire has burned up the burnt offering on the altar, and put them beside the altar. Then he is to take off these clothes, put on other clothes, and carry the ashes out of the camp to a ceremonially clean place. The fire on the altar must be kept burning and must not go out. Every morning the priest is to put more wood on it, lay out the burnt offering on it, and burn on it the fat from the peace offerings. Fire is to burn on the altar at all times, never going out. These are the instructions for the grain offering. Aaron’s sons are to present it before the LORD, in front of the altar. The priest is to take up a handful of the fine flour of the grain offering with some of its oil, along with all the frankincense on it, and burn it on the altar as its memorial portion, a soothing aroma to the LORD. What is left of it belongs to Aaron and his sons as food. They must eat it as bread made without yeast, and in a holy place: the courtyard of the tent of meeting is where they must eat it. It must not be baked with yeast. I have given it to them as their share of my food offerings. It is most holy, like the sin offering and the guilt offering. Any male descendant of Aaron may eat it. It is their permanent share of the food offerings to the LORD, for all your generations. Whoever touches these offerings will become holy.’”

The priests’ daily grain offering

The LORD spoke to Moses. He said, “This is the offering that Aaron and his sons are to present to the LORD from the day he is anointed: about 2 quarts of fine flour as a regular grain offering, half in the morning and half in the evening. It is to be made with oil on a griddle. Bring it in well soaked, and present it as a grain offering broken into pieces, a soothing aroma to the LORD. The son who succeeds him as the anointed priest is to prepare it. This is the LORD’s permanent due: it must be burned completely. Every grain offering a priest brings for himself is to be burned whole; it must not be eaten.”

Instructions for the sin offering

The LORD spoke to Moses. He said, “Speak to Aaron and his sons and tell them: ‘These are the instructions for the sin offering. The sin offering is to be slaughtered before the LORD at the same place where the burnt offering is slaughtered. It is most holy. The priest who offers it for sin is to eat it. It must be eaten in a holy place, in the courtyard of the tent of meeting. Whatever touches its meat will become holy. If any of its blood spatters on a garment, you must wash the stained part in a holy place. Any clay pot it is boiled in must be broken. If it is boiled in a bronze pot, the pot must be scrubbed and rinsed with water. Any male of priestly descent may eat it. It is most holy. But no sin offering is to be eaten if any of its blood has been brought into the tent of meeting to make atonement in the holy place. It must be burned in the fire.

fields.title: Leviticus 7
fields.body_html:
Instructions for the guilt offering

These are the instructions for the guilt offering. It is most holy. The guilt offering is to be slaughtered at the same place as the burnt offering, and the priest is to splash its blood all around on the altar. All its fat is to be offered from it: the fat tail, the fat that covers the internal organs, the two kidneys with the fat on them by the lower back, and the long lobe of the liver, which is to be taken out together with the kidneys. The priest is to turn them into smoke on the altar as a food offering to the LORD. It is a guilt offering. Any male of priestly descent may eat it. It must be eaten in a holy place. It is most holy. The guilt offering is like the sin offering: the same rule applies to both. The animal belongs to the priest who makes atonement with it. When a priest offers a burnt offering for someone, the hide of the animal he offered is his to keep. Any grain offering that has been baked in an oven, or prepared in a pan or on a griddle, is to go to the priest who presents it. Every other grain offering, whether mixed with oil or dry, belongs to all of Aaron’s sons, to be shared alike among them.

Instructions for the peace offering

These are the instructions for the peace offering that someone brings to the LORD. If it is brought to give thanks, the worshiper must also present, with the thanksgiving sacrifice, loaves made without yeast and mixed with oil, wafers made without yeast and spread with oil, and loaves of fine flour well soaked and mixed with oil. With their thanksgiving peace offering they are also to present loaves of bread made with yeast. From each kind of offering they are to present one loaf as a contribution to the LORD. It belongs to the priest who splashes the blood of the peace offering. The meat of the peace offering given in thanks is to be eaten the same day it is offered. Nothing of it is to be kept until the next morning. If the sacrifice is offered to fulfill a vow, or as a freewill offering, it is to be eaten on the day it is presented, and the rest may still be eaten the following day. But any meat from the sacrifice still left on the third day must be burned up. Should any meat of the peace offering be eaten on the third day, the one who brought it will not be accepted, and the offering will not count in their favor. It is foul meat, and whoever eats any of it will bear the guilt. If the meat comes into contact with anything unclean, no one may eat it; it must be burned in the fire. Otherwise, the meat may be eaten by anyone who is clean. If anyone who is unclean eats meat from a peace offering that belongs to the LORD, that person must be cut off from the people. If a person has touched anything unclean, such as human uncleanness, an unclean animal, or some unclean detestable creature, and then eats meat from the peace offering that belongs to the LORD, that person must be cut off from the people.’”

No fat and no blood

The LORD spoke to Moses. He said, “Speak to the Israelites and tell them: ‘You must not eat any fat from cattle, sheep or goats. The fat of an animal that died on its own, or that was torn apart by wild animals, can be put to any use, but you must on no account eat it. If anyone eats fat from an animal of the kind presented to the LORD as a food offering, the one who eats it must be cut off from the people. You must not eat any blood at all, whether from a bird or from an animal, wherever you live. Whoever eats any blood, that person must be cut off from the people.’”

The priests’ share of the peace offerings

The LORD spoke to Moses. He said, “Speak to the Israelites and tell them: ‘When anyone offers a peace offering to the LORD, they themselves must bring from it a gift for the LORD. The worshiper must carry the LORD’s food offerings in their own hands: the fat, together with the breast. The breast is for waving before the LORD as a wave offering. The fat the priest is to turn into smoke on the altar; the breast goes to Aaron and his sons. From your peace offerings you must also hand over the right thigh as a contribution for the priest. That thigh is the share of whichever of Aaron’s sons offers the blood and the fat of the peace offering. For I have taken the breast of the wave offering and the thigh of the contribution from the peace offerings of the Israelites, and have given them to Aaron the priest and his sons as their permanent share from the Israelites.’” This is the share of Aaron and his sons from the LORD’s food offerings, from the day they were presented to serve the LORD as priests, which the LORD commanded the Israelites to give them on the day they were anointed. It is a permanent rule for all their generations. These are the instructions for the burnt offering, the grain offering, the sin offering, the guilt offering, the ordination offering and the peace offering, which the LORD commanded Moses on Mount Sinai at the time he commanded the Israelites, in the wilderness of Sinai, to bring their offerings to the LORD.

fields.title: Leviticus 8
fields.body_html:
Aaron and his sons are ordained

The LORD spoke to Moses. He said, “Take Aaron, and his sons with him. Take also the garments, the anointing oil, the bull for the sin offering, the two rams, and the basket of bread made without yeast. Then call the whole congregation together at the entrance of the tent of meeting.” Moses followed the LORD’s command, and the congregation gathered at the entrance of the tent of meeting. Moses said to the congregation, “What you are about to see done is what the LORD has commanded.” Moses had Aaron and his sons come forward, and he washed them with water. He put the tunic on Aaron and tied the sash around his waist. He dressed him in the robe and put the ephod over it, then tied the ephod’s woven band around him, and so fastened the ephod on him. Over it he set the breastpiece, and inside the breastpiece he placed the Urim and the Thummim. He set the turban on Aaron’s head, and on the front of the turban he fixed the gold plate, the holy crown, just as the LORD had commanded Moses. Moses then took the anointing oil. He anointed the tabernacle and all that it held, and consecrated them. He sprinkled some of the oil seven times on the altar, and anointed the altar with all its utensils, and the basin with its stand, to consecrate them. He poured some of the anointing oil on Aaron’s head, anointing him to consecrate him. Then Moses had Aaron’s sons come forward. He dressed them in tunics, tied sashes around their waists, and fastened caps on their heads, just as the LORD had commanded Moses. He led up the bull for the sin offering, and Aaron and his sons laid their hands on its head. Moses slaughtered it, took the blood, and with his finger put some on each of the horns of the altar all around, purifying the altar. He poured out the rest of the blood at the base of the altar. So he consecrated it, to make atonement for it. He took all the fat on the internal organs, the long lobe of the liver, and both kidneys with their fat, and Moses burned them on the altar. But the bull, with its hide, its meat and its dung, he burned up outside the camp, just as the LORD had commanded Moses. Then he brought forward the ram for the burnt offering, and Aaron and his sons laid their hands on its head. Moses slaughtered it and splashed the blood against all sides of the altar. He cut the ram into its pieces, and Moses burned the head, the pieces and the fat. He washed the internal organs and the legs in water, and Moses burned the whole ram on the altar. It was a burnt offering with a soothing aroma, a food offering to the LORD, just as the LORD had commanded Moses. Next he brought forward the other ram, the ram of ordination, and Aaron and his sons laid their hands on its head. Moses slaughtered it and took some of its blood. He put it on the lobe of Aaron’s right ear, on the thumb of his right hand and on the big toe of his right foot. Then he had Aaron’s sons come forward, and Moses put some of the blood on the lobes of their right ears, on the thumbs of their right hands and on the big toes of their right feet. And Moses splashed the blood against all sides of the altar. He took the fat: the fat tail, all the fat on the internal organs, the long lobe of the liver, both kidneys with their fat, and also the right thigh. From the basket of bread made without yeast that stood before the LORD he took one loaf made without yeast, one loaf made with oil, and one wafer, and laid them on the fat portions and on the right thigh. He put all of this in the hands of Aaron and his sons and waved it before the LORD as a wave offering. Then Moses took them back from their hands and burned them on the altar on top of the burnt offering. They were an ordination offering with a soothing aroma, a food offering to the LORD. Moses took the breast and waved it before the LORD as a wave offering. It was Moses’ own share of the ram of ordination, just as the LORD had commanded Moses. Moses took some of the anointing oil and some of the blood on the altar and sprinkled it on Aaron and his garments, and on his sons and their garments. In this way he consecrated Aaron and his garments, and his sons and their garments with him. Moses told Aaron and his sons, “Boil the meat at the entrance of the tent of meeting and eat it there, with the bread that is in the ordination basket, as I commanded when I said, ‘Aaron and his sons are to eat it.’ Whatever is left of the meat and the bread you must burn up. Stay at the entrance of the tent of meeting and do not leave it for seven days, until the time of your ordination is over. It will take seven days for you to be ordained. What has been done today, the LORD has commanded to be done again, to make atonement for you. Remain at the entrance of the tent of meeting day and night for seven days, and keep the watch the LORD has given you, so that you will not die. This is the command I have received.” Aaron and his sons carried out everything the LORD had commanded through Moses.

fields.title: Leviticus 9
fields.body_html:
Aaron offers the first sacrifices

When the eighth day came, Moses called for Aaron and his sons and for the elders of Israel. He told Aaron, “Choose a young calf from the herd as a sin offering for yourself, and a ram as a burnt offering, each without defect, and bring them before the LORD. And say to the Israelites, ‘Bring a male goat for a sin offering, and for a burnt offering a calf and a lamb, year-old animals without defect, and an ox and a ram to be sacrificed before the LORD as a peace offering, and a grain offering mixed with oil. For the LORD will appear to you today.’” So they brought everything Moses had commanded to the area in front of the tent of meeting, and the whole congregation approached and stood there before the LORD. Moses said, “Do this, as the LORD has commanded, and the glory of the LORD will appear to you.” Then Moses told Aaron, “Approach the altar. Offer your sin offering and your burnt offering, and so make atonement for yourself and for the people. Then present the people’s offering and make atonement for them, just as the LORD has commanded.” So Aaron went to the altar and slaughtered the calf for his own sin offering. Aaron’s sons handed him the blood. He dipped his finger in it and put some on the horns of the altar, and he poured out the rest of the blood at the base of the altar. Then on the altar he burned the fat, the kidneys and the long lobe of the liver from the sin offering, as the LORD had commanded Moses. He burned the meat and the hide in a fire outside the camp. Then Aaron slaughtered the burnt offering. When his sons passed the blood to him, he splashed it on every side of the altar. His sons passed him the pieces of the burnt offering one by one, and the head as well, and he burned it all on the altar. The internal organs and the legs he washed, then burned them on the altar on top of the rest of the burnt offering. After that Aaron brought the people’s offering forward. He took the goat for their sin offering, slaughtered it, and offered it as a sin offering in the same way as the first. He also brought forward the burnt offering and offered it as the rule required. Then he presented the grain offering. He filled his hand with some of it and burned that on the altar, in addition to the morning burnt offering. Next he slaughtered the ox and the ram, the peace offering for the people. When Aaron’s sons passed him the blood, he splashed it on every side of the altar. The fat portions from the ox and the ram, the fat tail, the fat that covers the internal organs, the kidneys and the long lobe of the liver, these fat portions they laid on top of the breasts. Then Aaron burned the fat on the altar. As for the breasts and the right thigh, Aaron waved them before the LORD as a wave offering, following Moses’ command. Aaron then held out his hands toward the people and blessed them. And when he had finished presenting the sin offering, the burnt offering and the peace offering, he came down from the altar. Moses and Aaron entered the tent of meeting, and on coming out again they blessed the people. Then the glory of the LORD appeared to all the people. Fire went out from before the LORD and devoured the burnt offering and the fat portions lying on the altar. When all the people saw it, they cried out with joy and bowed down with their faces to the ground.

fields.title: Leviticus 10
fields.body_html:
The death of Nadab and Abihu

Aaron’s sons Nadab and Abihu each took his own censer. They put fire in it, laid incense on the fire, and offered before the LORD an improper fire, one he had not commanded them to bring. Then fire went out from before the LORD and devoured them, and they died in the presence of the LORD. Moses said to Aaron, “This is what the LORD meant when he said, ‘Through those who come near me I will show that I am holy, and in the sight of all the people I will show my glory.’” And Aaron said nothing. Moses sent for Mishael and Elzaphan, the sons of Uzziel, who was Aaron’s uncle. He told them, “Come forward and take your relatives from in front of the sanctuary, and carry them out of the camp.” They came forward and carried them out of the camp in their own tunics, just as Moses had said. Then Moses said to Aaron and his sons Eleazar and Ithamar, “Do not let your hair hang loose or tear your clothes in mourning, or you will die, and he will be angry with the whole congregation. Your relatives, the whole house of Israel, may weep over the burning the LORD has brought about. Do not leave your place at the entrance of the tent of meeting, or you will die, because you bear the LORD’s anointing oil.” They did as Moses said.

No wine for priests on duty

The LORD spoke to Aaron. He said, “Whenever you or your sons go into the tent of meeting, you must drink no wine or beer, or you will die. This is a permanent rule for all your generations, so that you can tell apart what is holy and what is common, what is unclean and what is clean, and so that you can teach the Israelites all the rules the LORD has given them through Moses.”

Eating the priests’ share

Moses said to Aaron and to his sons who were left, Eleazar and Ithamar, “Take the grain offering that remains from the LORD’s food offerings and eat it, made without yeast, beside the altar, because it is most holy. Eat it in a holy place, because it is the share set aside for you and your sons from the LORD’s food offerings. This is what I have been commanded. But the breast of the wave offering and the thigh given as a contribution you may eat in any ceremonially clean place, you and your sons and daughters with you. They have been given to you and your children as your share from the peace offerings of the Israelites. The thigh of the contribution and the breast of the wave offering are to be brought along with the fat portions for the food offerings, and waved before the LORD as a wave offering. They will belong to you and to your sons with you as your permanent share, as the LORD has commanded.” Moses made a careful search for the goat of the sin offering, and it turned out that it had been burned. He was angry with Eleazar and Ithamar, the two sons of Aaron who were left, and he said, “Why did you not eat the sin offering in the holy area? It is most holy, and he has given it to you so that you may carry the guilt of the congregation and make atonement for them before the LORD. Its blood was not brought inside the sanctuary, so you certainly should have eaten the goat in the holy area, as I commanded.” Aaron answered Moses, “Look, this very day they brought their sin offering and their burnt offering before the LORD, and still such things have happened to me. Had I eaten sin offering today, would that have been right in the eyes of the LORD?” When Moses heard this, it seemed right to him.

fields.title: Leviticus 11
fields.body_html:
Clean and unclean animals

The LORD spoke to Moses and Aaron. He said to them, “Speak to the Israelites and tell them: ‘Of all the animals that live on land, these are the creatures you may eat. You may eat any animal that both chews the cud and has hooves split fully in two. Yet you must not eat these, even though they chew the cud or have split hooves: the camel, because it chews the cud but its hoof is not split. It is unclean for you. The rock badger chews the cud, but its hoof is not split; it is unclean for you. The hare also chews the cud, but its hoof is not split; it is unclean for you. The pig has hooves split fully in two, but it does not chew the cud; it is unclean for you. Do not eat any of their meat, and do not touch them when they are dead. They are unclean for you. These are the water creatures you may eat: whatever has fins and scales, whether it lives in the seas or in the streams. But anything in the seas or streams without fins and scales, whether it is one of the small creatures that swarm in the water or any other living thing there, is to be detestable to you. They are to remain detestable to you. Do not eat their meat, and treat their dead bodies as detestable. Whatever lives in the water without fins and scales is to be detestable to you. Among the birds, these are the ones you are to detest. They must not be eaten, because they are detestable: the eagle, the bearded vulture, the black vulture, the red kite, the various kinds of black kite, every kind of raven, the ostrich, the screech owl, the gull, the various kinds of falcon, the little owl, the cormorant, the eagle owl, the barn owl, the desert owl, the carrion vulture, the stork, the various kinds of heron, the hoopoe and the bat. Any swarming creature with wings that also walks on all fours is to be detestable to you.

Winged swarming creatures and carcasses

But you may eat some of the winged swarming creatures that walk on all fours: those that have a pair of long legs above their feet for hopping across the ground. Of these you may eat the following, each by its own kind: the swarming locust, the bald locust, the cricket and the grasshopper. Every other winged swarming creature that goes on four feet is to be detestable to you. These too will make you unclean. Whoever touches the dead body of one of them will be unclean until evening. Anyone who carries any part of their dead bodies must wash their clothes, and they remain unclean until evening. Every animal with hooves that are not split all the way through, and that does not chew the cud, is unclean for you. Anyone who touches one when it is dead will become unclean. Every four-footed creature that walks on the pads of its feet is unclean for you. Anyone who touches the carcass of one will be unclean until evening. Whoever carries their carcass must wash their clothes and will be unclean until evening. These animals are unclean for you.

Small creatures that swarm on the ground

Of the small creatures that swarm on the ground, these are unclean for you: the weasel, the mouse, the various kinds of great lizard, the gecko, the monitor lizard, the wall lizard, the sand lizard and the chameleon. These are the swarming creatures that are unclean for you. If anyone touches one of them once it is dead, that person will be unclean until evening. Anything that one of them falls on after it has died becomes unclean: any wooden object, any clothing, leather or sackcloth, any tool or article used for work. It must be dipped in water and will remain unclean until evening; after that it is clean. If one of them falls inside a pot made of clay, all that is in the pot becomes unclean, and the pot itself must be smashed. Any food that could be eaten becomes unclean if water from such a pot has come on it, and any drink in such a pot becomes unclean. Anything touched by part of their carcass when it falls becomes unclean. If it is an oven or a stove, it must be torn down. These are unclean, and you are to keep treating them as unclean. Water in a spring or a cistern, where water is gathered, stays clean. But whoever touches the carcass will be unclean. Seed for planting stays clean even if part of a carcass falls on it. If the seed has been soaked in water, though, and part of a carcass falls on it, you must treat it as unclean.

Carcasses, and the call to be holy

When an animal of the kind you may eat dies on its own, whoever touches the carcass will be unclean until evening. Someone who eats any of its carcass is to wash their clothes and will be unclean until evening. The same applies to someone who carries the carcass: they are to wash their clothes and will be unclean until evening. All the small creatures that swarm on the ground are detestable and are not to be eaten. Nothing that swarms on the ground may be eaten, whether it crawls on its belly, goes on four legs, or has a great many legs. They are detestable. Do not make yourselves detestable through any creature that swarms. Do not make yourselves unclean by them, so that you become unclean through them. For I am the LORD your God. Consecrate yourselves, then. You must be holy, because I am holy. None of the creatures that creep on the ground must make you unclean. For I am the LORD, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt to be your God. You must be holy, because I am holy. These are the instructions for land animals, birds, every living creature that moves through the waters, and every creature that swarms on the ground, so that you can tell the unclean from the clean, the creatures that may be eaten from those that may not.’”

fields.title: Leviticus 12
fields.body_html:
Purification after childbirth

The LORD spoke to Moses. He said, “Speak to the Israelites and tell them: ‘When a woman becomes pregnant and gives birth to a boy, she will be unclean for seven days. She will be unclean just as she is during her monthly period. On the eighth day the boy is to be circumcised. She is then to remain thirty-three days in the time of her blood purification. Until those days are over, she must not touch anything holy or come into the sanctuary. If she gives birth to a girl, she will be unclean for two weeks, as she is during her monthly period. She is then to remain sixty-six days in the time of her blood purification. When the days of her purification are over, whether for a son or a daughter, she is to bring to the priest, at the entrance of the tent of meeting, a lamb a year old for a burnt offering and a young pigeon or a turtledove for a sin offering. He is to present it before the LORD and make atonement for her, and then she will be clean from her flow of blood. This is the law for a woman who gives birth to a boy or a girl. If she cannot afford a lamb, she is to take two turtledoves or two young pigeons, one for a burnt offering and the other for a sin offering. The priest will make atonement for her, and she will be clean.’”

fields.title: Leviticus 13
fields.body_html:
Serious skin disease

The LORD spoke to Moses and Aaron. He said, “If a swelling, a scab or a bright spot appears on the skin of someone’s body and turns into what may be a sore of serious skin disease, the person is to be brought to Aaron the priest or to one of his sons, the priests. The priest is to look closely at the sore. If the hair in it has turned white and it seems to go deeper than the surface of the skin, it is a sore of serious skin disease. Once he has seen it, the priest is to declare the person unclean. If, however, there is a white bright spot on the skin that does not seem to go below the surface, and its hair has not turned white, the priest is to shut the person away for seven days. On the seventh day the priest is to look at the person again. If in his judgment the sore is unchanged and has not spread in the skin, he is to shut them away for another seven days. When the second seven days are over, the priest is to look once more. If the sore has grown dim and not spread over the skin, it is merely a scab, and the priest is to declare the person clean. After washing their clothes, they are clean. But if the scab spreads in the skin after they have shown themselves to the priest and been declared clean, they must come before the priest again. If the priest sees that the scab has spread in the skin, he is to declare the person unclean: it is a serious skin disease.

Anyone who has a sore of serious skin disease is to be brought to the priest. The priest is to look. If there is a white swelling in the skin that has turned the hair white, and there is raw flesh in the swelling, it is a long-standing serious skin disease in the skin of the body. The priest is to declare the person unclean without shutting them away, for there is no doubt that they are unclean. If the disease breaks out all over the skin and covers the whole skin of the person with the sore, from head to foot, wherever the priest looks, the priest is to look, and if the disease has covered the whole body, he is to declare the person clean. It has all turned white; they are clean. But whenever raw flesh appears on them, they will be unclean. The priest is to look at the raw flesh and declare the person unclean. Raw flesh is unclean; it is a serious skin disease. But if the raw flesh changes again and turns white, they are to go to the priest. The priest is to examine them, and if the sore has turned white, he is to declare the person with the sore clean. They are clean.

Boils and burns

When someone has a boil on their skin and it has healed, and a white swelling or a reddish-white bright spot appears where the boil was, they are to show it to the priest. The priest is to examine it. If it looks lower than the skin around it and its hair has turned white, the priest is to declare the person unclean. It is a sore of serious skin disease that has broken out where the boil was. But if the priest finds no white hair in it, and it is not lower than the skin, and it has faded, he is to shut the person away for seven days. If it spreads in the skin, the priest is to declare the person unclean. It is a sore of the disease. If the bright spot stays put and does not spread, it is the boil’s scar, and the priest is to declare the person clean.

Or when someone has a burn on their skin, and the raw place of the burn becomes a reddish-white or white bright spot, the priest is to look at it. If the hair in the bright spot has turned white and the spot looks deeper than the skin, it is a serious skin disease that has broken out in the burn. The priest is to declare the person unclean; it is a sore of serious skin disease. But if the priest finds no white hair in the bright spot, and it is not lower than the skin, and it has faded, he is to shut the person away for seven days. On the seventh day the priest is to look at them. If it has spread in the skin, the priest is to declare the person unclean; it is a sore of serious skin disease. But if the bright spot stays where it is, has not spread in the skin, and has faded, it is the swelling from the burn. The priest is to declare the person clean, because it is the scar of the burn.

Sores on the head or in the beard

When a man or a woman has a sore on the head or in the beard, the priest is to examine the sore. If it looks deeper than the skin and there is thin yellow hair in it, the priest is to declare the person unclean. It is a scaly itch, a serious skin disease of the head or beard. But if the priest examines the sore of the scaly itch and it does not look deeper than the skin, and there is no black hair in it, he is to shut the person with the sore away for seven days. On the seventh day the priest is to look at the sore. If the scaly itch has not spread, and no yellow hair has appeared in it, and it does not look deeper than the skin, the person is to shave, but not the place where the scaly itch is, and the priest is to shut them away for another seven days. On the seventh day the priest is to look at the scaly itch. If it has not spread in the skin and does not look deeper than the skin, he is to declare the person clean. They must wash their clothes, and they will be clean. But if the scaly itch does spread in the skin after they have been declared clean, and the priest examines them and finds that it has spread in the skin, he need not look for yellow hair. The person is unclean. But if in the priest’s judgment the scaly itch is unchanged, and black hair has grown in it, it has healed. The person is clean, and the priest is to declare them clean.

Rashes and baldness

When a man or a woman has bright spots on the skin, white bright spots, and the priest finds that the spots on their skin are a dull white, it is a rash, nothing more, breaking out on the skin. The person is clean.

When a man loses the hair of his head, he is bald, but he is clean. If he loses the hair at the front of his head, he is bald at the forehead, but he is clean. But if a reddish-white sore appears on his bald head or forehead, it is a serious skin disease breaking out on his bald head or forehead. The priest is to examine him. If the swollen sore on his bald head or forehead is reddish-white, looking like a serious skin disease on the body, he is a man with a serious skin disease and he is unclean. The priest must declare him unclean; the sore is on his head. The person who has the sore of serious skin disease is to go about in torn clothes, with the hair of the head left loose. They are to cover their upper lip and shout, ‘Unclean, unclean!’ For the whole time the sore is on them they are unclean. Being unclean, they are to live by themselves, making their home outside the camp.

Mold in clothing and leather

When a patch of mold is found in clothing, whether wool or linen clothing, or in the warp or the weft of linen or wool, or in leather or anything made of leather, and the patch in the clothing or leather, in the warp or weft, or in any leather article is greenish or reddish, it is a patch of mold and must be shown to the priest. The priest is to examine the patch and shut the article away for seven days. On the seventh day he is to look at the patch. If it has spread in the clothing, the warp or weft, or the leather, whatever the leather is used for, it is a spreading mold, and the article is unclean. He must burn the clothing, the woolen or linen warp or weft, or the leather article that has the patch in it. Because it is a spreading mold, it must be burned up. But if the priest examines it and the patch has not spread in the clothing, the warp or weft, or the leather article, the priest is to order the article with the patch washed and shut it away for another seven days. After it has been washed, the priest is to look at the patch again. If its appearance has not changed, even though it has not spread, it is unclean. You must burn it; it is a rot that has eaten into the back or the front of it. But if the priest looks and the patch has faded after being washed, he is to tear the patch out of the clothing, the leather, or the warp or weft. If it appears again in the clothing, the warp or weft, or the leather article, it is breaking out afresh, and you must burn whatever has the patch in it. But the clothing, the warp or weft, or the leather article that you wash and from which the patch has gone, is to be washed a second time, and it will be clean. This is the law for mold in clothing of wool or linen, in the warp or weft, or in any article of leather, for declaring it clean or unclean.”

fields.title: Leviticus 14
fields.body_html:
Cleansing from serious skin disease

The LORD spoke to Moses. He said, “This is the law for a person with a serious skin disease, for the day they are to be made clean. They are to be brought to the priest. The priest is to go out of the camp and look the person over. If the sore of the serious skin disease has healed, the priest is to have someone take, for the one being cleansed, two clean birds that are alive, with some cedar wood, scarlet yarn and hyssop. At the priest’s order one of the birds is to be slaughtered over fresh water held in a clay pot. Then he is to take the live bird and the cedar wood, the scarlet yarn and the hyssop, and dip them all, live bird too, into the blood of the bird that was killed over the fresh water. He is to sprinkle the one being cleansed from the serious skin disease seven times and declare them clean. Then he is to set the live bird free in the open country. Then the one being cleansed is to wash their clothes, shave off all their hair, and bathe in water, and so become clean. After that they may enter the camp, but for seven days they are to live outside their own tent. On the seventh day they are to shave again, all of it: the hair of the head, the beard, the eyebrows, every hair on the body. They are to wash their clothes and bathe their body in water, and they will be clean. On the eighth day they are to take two male lambs without defect and one year-old ewe lamb without defect, with about 6 quarts of fine flour mixed with oil as a grain offering, and about a third of a quart of oil. The priest who is declaring them clean is to set the person being cleansed, and these offerings, before the LORD at the entrance of the tent of meeting. The priest is to take one of the male lambs and present it as a guilt offering, together with the log of oil, and lift them up and wave them as a wave offering before the LORD. He is to slaughter the lamb at the place in the holy area where the sin offering and the burnt offering are slaughtered. The guilt offering goes to the priest, just as the sin offering does; it is most holy. The priest is to take some of the guilt offering’s blood and put it on the right earlobe of the person being cleansed, on their right thumb, and on the big toe of their right foot. Next the priest is to take some of the log of oil and pour it into the palm of his own left hand. The priest is to dip his right forefinger into the oil in his left palm, and with his finger sprinkle some of the oil seven times before the LORD. Some of the oil still in his palm the priest is to put on the right earlobe of the person being cleansed, on their right thumb, and on the big toe of their right foot, over the blood of the guilt offering. What is left of the oil in the priest’s palm he is to put on the head of the person being cleansed. So the priest will make atonement for them before the LORD. The priest is then to offer the sin offering and make atonement for the person being cleansed from their uncleanness. After that he is to slaughter the burnt offering. He is to offer up the burnt offering and the grain offering on the altar. So the priest will make atonement for them, and they will be clean.

Cleansing for someone who is poor

If they are poor and cannot afford this much, they are to take one male lamb as a guilt offering to be waved, to make atonement for them, with about 2 quarts of fine flour mixed with oil as a grain offering, and about a third of a quart of oil, and also two turtledoves or two young pigeons, whichever they can afford, one for a sin offering and the other for a burnt offering. On the eighth day they are to bring them for their cleansing to the priest at the entrance of the tent of meeting, before the LORD. The priest is to take the lamb for the guilt offering and the log of oil and lift them up and wave them as a wave offering before the LORD. He is to slaughter the lamb of the guilt offering, take some of its blood, and put it on the right earlobe of the person being cleansed, on their right thumb, and on the big toe of their right foot. The priest is to pour some of the oil into the palm of his own left hand. With his right forefinger he is to sprinkle some of the oil in his left palm seven times before the LORD. The priest is to put some of the oil in his palm on the right earlobe of the person being cleansed, on their right thumb, and on the big toe of their right foot, the same places where the blood of the guilt offering was put. What is left of the oil in the priest’s palm he is to put on the head of the person being cleansed, to make atonement for them before the LORD. Then he is to offer the turtledoves or the young pigeons, whichever the person can afford, the means they have: one for a sin offering and the other for a burnt offering, along with the grain offering. So the priest will make atonement for the person being cleansed before the LORD. This is the law for anyone who has had a serious skin disease and cannot afford the usual offerings for their cleansing.”

Mold in a house

The LORD spoke to Moses and Aaron. He said, “When you enter the land of Canaan, which I am giving you to own, and I put a patch of mold in a house in the land you own, the owner of the house is to come and tell the priest, ‘I have seen what looks like a patch of mold in my house.’ The priest is to order the house emptied before he goes in to examine the patch, so that nothing in the house becomes unclean. After that the priest is to go in and look at the house. He is to look at the patch. If it is in the walls of the house, as greenish or reddish hollows that look deeper than the surface of the wall, the priest is to go out of the house to its doorway and close the house up for seven days. On the seventh day the priest is to come back and look.
